entries.title: Eco wins: Cities, creatures, and tech are saving the day
entries.summary: From an AI-powered cute little pangolin, heat mapping to cool down cities and animals reducing wildfire risks by doing their thing, these real-world climate hacks are helping communities stay ahead of a changing planet.
entries.content:
Nature and EnvironmentGlobal issues

Eco wins: Cities, creatures, and tech are saving the day

July 25, 2026

From an AI-powered cute little pangolin, heat mapping to cool down cities and animals reducing wildfire risks by doing their thing, these real-world climate hacks are helping communities stay ahead of a changing planet.

Nature's own firefighters

Sometimes the best climate solutions have four legs. From goats and sheep in the United States to donkeys in Spain, grazing animals are helping reduce wildfire risk by clearing dry vegetation that can fuel fires.

Carefully managed grazing not only slows the spread of potential wildfires but can also create access paths for emergency crews. It's a simple yet effective example of how working with nature can help communities become more resilient to a changing climate. 

Keeping cities cool: Reclaiming the right to a livable future

Young voices and urban innovators are driving change in the fight against extreme heat. Climate activist Che Chen is taking Taiwan's government to court because he believes access to a livable, cooler environment is a basic human right for his generation and those to come.

At the same time, urban heat expert Tzu-ping Lin is developing practical solutions such as wind corridors, greener buildings and heat mapping to make cities more resilient.

One of the world's most threatened animals speaks up

Conservationists and storytellers are finding new ways to connect people with endangered wildlife in South Africa by helping audiences imagine the world through the eyes of a pangolin.

The cute, AI-powered creature speaks South Africa's 11 official languages, answers questions, reacts realistically and ultimately highlights the threats facing the world's most trafficked mammal, which is poached primarily for its meat and scales.

The initiative is driven by a desire to inspire empathy and action, showing that protecting biodiversity starts with understanding the species we share our planet with.

Edited by: Sarah Steffen

entries.title: India: CJP-Government to return to talks as protests grow
entries.summary: The Cockroack Janta Party-led protests are likely to swell in size over the weekend as office-goers join in. Meanwhile, a second round of talks with the government are scheduled for later today. DW has more.
entries.content:
India

India: CJP-Government to return to talks as protests grow

Published July 25, 2026last updated July 25, 2026

The Cockroack Janta Party-led protests are likely to swell in size over the weekend as office-goers join in. Meanwhile, a second round of talks with the government are scheduled for later today. DW has more.

Skip next section What you need to know

What you need to know

  • Second round of talks between Cockroach movementand Indian government scheduled
  • Police tighten security as crowds expected to swell over weekend
  • Cockroach Janta Party Founder Abhijeet Dipke says diagnosed with typhoid

Here's a roundup of the biggest headlines from India on Saturday, July 25: 

Tired of missing our real-time updates? Click here to add us as a Preferred Source on Google. Then tap the "Star" or "Preferred" to keep DW News at the top of your feed.

Skip next section CJP calls for nationwide candle march on Sunday

CJP calls for nationwide candle march on Sunday

The Cockroach movement has called for a nationwide candle march on Sunday evening, as it looks to keep up the pressure on the Narendra Modi government.

"One person, one candle. For every student the government failed. March together in silence," the poster said.

That is despite ongoing talks between the movement's spokespeople and the government. CJP leaders and protesters on the ground have said that they will keep taking to the streets until Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan resigns.

Critics of the movement have pointed out that the government has arrested several reported to be involved in the paper leak scandal. Moreover, paper leaks have long happened in India even under previous governments. A common arguments is that removing a minister would not make a difference.

Countering this, protesters and their supporters have said that as education minister, the buck stops with Pradhan. CJP leaders have repeated that the minister must take accountability for the leak, which reportedly pushed at least 20 students to suicide. 

Skip next section PM Modi 'thanks friends' in another late night video

PM Modi 'thanks friends' in another late night video

Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi uploaded yet another reel overnight — this time thanking "friends" for their suggestions over a Gen-Z style video posted late the night before.

"I had a chance to meet you all late last night. The response to the video I posted, the insightful suggestions... thank you everybody," he said in the latest video.

In the previous reel, the prime minister had appealed to the nation that the government had taken several steps to counter the paper leak issue. It was one of his lesser-produced videos shot in a less-than ideal angle, seemingly in an attempt to connect with the youth.

Many protesters on ground read the video as a "desperate attempt" to manage the students' anger as protests began to spread nationwide. "He suddenly woke up and posted a panic reel because they didn't expect the protests to reach this stage," one protesters told DW, asking to stay anonymous over fear of backlash.

Meanwhile, social media did what it does best and made memes.

The Prime Minister appears to have acknowledged that he is watching and learning.

Skip next section IN PICTURES: Overnight scenes from the protest at Jantar Mantar

IN PICTURES: Overnight scenes from the protest at Jantar Mantar

Skip next section CJP Founder Abhijeet Dipke diagnosed with typhoid

CJP Founder Abhijeet Dipke diagnosed with typhoid

Political pressure group Cockroack Janta Party's leader and Founder Abhijeet Dipke has been diagnosed with typhoid, he said in the early hours of Saturday in a post on X.

"I have been diagnosed with typhoid. My treatment is on, I am being administered IV [fluids] day and night," Dipke said, holding up his hand to show the catheter set up.

"But I really want to thank the cockroaches which have been protesting peacefully across the nation and have made this movement so successful. A big, big thankyou to all and congratulation to you all for such a big,big success. And I am very sure if we continue protesting peacefully, Dharmendra Pradhan will have to resign," he said, speaking of the education minister.

Dipke and several protesters have been camping at the Jantar Mantar protest site since over a month now. 

Skip next section WATCH: Delhi police crack down on student protests

WATCH: Delhi police crack down on student protests

There have been accusations of police brutality in New Delhi after police used tear gas and batons against anti-government protesters from the "Cockroach" movement.

The mood among protesters is rather tense, DW correspondent Adil Bhat reports. People gather in large numbers, chant slogans and demand the resignation of India's education minister, Dharmendra Pradhan.

The current protest movement is not tied to any ideology, he adds: "it will continue even if there is no leadership."

Skip next section Government-CJP second round of talks set for Saturday evening

Government-CJP second round of talks set for Saturday evening

Cockroach Janta Partyspokesperson and Indian government respresentatives are set to meet for the second round of talks on Saturday evening, after first round of talks on Friday did not lead to a breakthrough. 

This comes amid youth-led nationwide protests in India against a struggling education system and Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan, after a national medical enterance exam's question papers leaked in May.

The leak affected millions of medical aspirants and is believed to have led to several students committing suicide.

"They had given us the time for 3:30-4:00 p.m. (1000 GMT-1030 GMT) today. The location has not been finalised yet," CJP National Spokesperson Ashutosh Ranka told news agency ANI.

"Discussions are very clear. We should get written confirmation for the two demands on which there has been in-principle agreement. So that they can be closed. We need clarity over Dharmendra Pradhan — whether they will seek his resignation or not. We want an answer in Yes or No because there is not much scope for deliberation over this," he said.

On Friday, CJP's chief spokesperson Saurav Das and Ranka met Union Ministers Jagat Prakash Nadda and Jitender Singh at "neutral ground."

The ministers were presented CJP's three core demands: Pradhan's resignation, monetary compensation for the families of the students who committed suicide and no legal action against peaceful protesters.

The ministers reportedly sought a day's time to respond on the resignation demand and agreed to the other two.

Skip next section Welcome to our coverage

Welcome to our coverage

Hello and welcome to DW's India blog.

This is Mahima Kapoor reporting from the New Delhi bureau and I will be your guide through the massive student-led protests which began in the capital and are now spreading across the nation.

This is a high stakes weekend. Prime Minister Narendra Modi's government is set to hold a second round of talks with Cockroack Janta Party spokespeople on Saturday evening.

Remember, yesterday government representatives had asked for a day's time to respond on the movement's central demand — the resignation of Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan.

Protesters in central Delhi continue to show up in large numbers which are expected to grow even more into the weekend.

Meanwhile, Modi's cabinet approved amendments to a paper leak legislation with stricter punishments and fines for those convicted. The bill could be introduced in the Indian Parliament as soon as Monday.

Tune in for all of this and more.

entries.title: Iran war: Houthis vow response to 'dangerous escalation' by Saudi Arabia
entries.summary: Iran-backed Houthi rebels in Yemen claim that civilian sites were targeted in Saudi strikes on the Yemeni port city of Hodeida. Saudi Arabia says it hit military targets. DW has more.
entries.content:
Middle East

Iran war: Houthis vow response to Saudi strikes on Hodeida

Published July 25, 2026last updated July 25, 2026

Iran-backed Houthi rebels in Yemen claim that civilian sites were targeted in Saudi strikes on the Yemeni port city of Hodeida. Saudi Arabia says it hit military targets. DW has more.

Skip next section What you need to know

What you need to know

  • Houthi rebels in Yemen say Friday's Saudi strikes on the port city of Hodeida hit civilian infrastructure, injuring two people
  • Saudi Arabia says it will do everything necessary to protect its shipping amid a Houthi-enforced maritime blockade in the Red Sea
  • A flare-up between Iran-backed Houthis and Saudi Arabia, and the consequent disruption of shipping in the Red Sea, could worsen the global economic fallout from the war

Here are the latest developments from the Iran war and the wider Middle East on Saturday, July 25:

Tired of missing our real-time updates? Click here to add us as a Preferred Source on Google. Then tap the "Star" or "Preferred" to keep DW News at the top of your feed.

Skip next section Air defense system operated by Greek military downs missiles over Saudi Arabia — report

Air defense system operated by Greek military downs missiles over Saudi Arabia — report

An air ‌defense ⁠system ⁠operated ​by Greek military ​personnel in ​Saudi ‌Arabia intercepted ‌two ballistic missiles ‌launched ​from Yemen on Saturday, news agency Reuters cited Greek security sources as saying.

The missiles were targeting oil refineries ⁠in ​Yanbu, Reuters added.

Reuters reported that the interception ⁠was ​the second time that Greek military personnel had operated the system.

Since 2021, an bilateral defense agreement to protect Saudi Arabia's critical energy infrastructure has seen Greece deploy a US-made Patriot air defense battery, operated by Hellenic Air Force personnel.

Earlier in the morning, the Saudi Civil Defense had alerted residents of Yanbu about a "potential danger" in the governorate, without giving any further details. It later advised the public that the said danger had passed.

A series of strikes and counter-strikes by Yemen's Houthi rebels and Saudi Arabia have opened a new front in a war that has gripped the Middle East following US-Israeli strikes on Iran in February.

Skip next section Why Iran's Pickaxe Mountain is a tough target for the US

Why Iran's Pickaxe Mountain is a tough target for the US

A mysterious underground complex near Iran's Natanz nuclear facility is drawing global attention after US President Donald Trump suggested it could become the target of a military strike, with Trump claiming there may be uranium centrifuges located at the site.

Tehran has released almost no information about the complex burrowed under what is known in Farsi as "Kuh-e Kolang Gaz La," or Pickaxe Mountain.

Although the site has surfaced repeatedly in reports over the past few years, its purpose remains unclear. That uncertainty has made it one of the most closely watched locations linked to Iran's nuclear activities.

Read more here.

.

Skip next section WATCH: Is the US prepared for the 'major military punishment' that Trump has promised Iran?

WATCH: Is the US prepared for the 'major military punishment' that Trump has promised Iran?

President Donald Trump says the US and Iran are talking but Tehran is not yet ready for a peace deal. Trump says the US is ‘locked and loaded’ and has threatened to intensify attacks against Iran which it has launched daily since the ceasefire broke down two weeks ago. 

Skip next section Houthis claim missile attack in Saudi Arabia's south

Houthis claim missile attack in Saudi Arabia's south

Yemen's Houthi rebels have claimed a missile attack on the southern Saudi city of Jizan.

The Iran-backed group's Ansarollah media posted on Telegram early Saturday that fires had broken out in Jizan after a "Yemeni missile attack."

The militant group had earlier accused US-ally Riyadh of a "dangerous escalation"and warned that its actions "will not go unanswered."

A Saudi Civil defense alert said "danger has passed in Jazan Province," without mentioning a missile strike.

It issued another warning for "potential danger" in the Yanbu governorate.

Skip next section Yemen's Houthis vow retaliation for Saudi strikes

Yemen's Houthis vow retaliation for Saudi strikes

The Iran-backed Houthi rebels in Yemen have accused Saudi Arabia of targeting civilian infrastructure, amid an escalating flare-up with Riyadh.

Saudi Arabia on Friday hit the Houthi-held port city of Hodeida with strikes, the Saudi-led coalition in Yemen said, in response to the rebel group attacking Saudi oil tankers in the Red Sea as part of a maritime blockade.

"The Saudi enemy's targeting of civilian facilities in Hodeida and Kamaran island constitutes a dangerous escalation," the Houthis' Ansarollah media posted on Telegram.

"We affirm that these recent crimes will not go unanswered."

Houthi-run Al Masirah television said on Saturday that Saudi strikes had targeted facilities belonging to the state telecommunications corporation and Kamaran island, off Yemen's western coast.

The broadcaster reported that one worker was wounded in Hodeida while a woman was also injured on Kamaran Island.

The Saudi-led coalition, meanwhile, claimed that it hit "Houthi military sites" and destroyed targets that were posing a threat to commercial vessels in the Red Sea.

Riyadh said it would do everything necessary to protect its ships, warning the Houthis that if they continued "hostile acts then there will be no hesitation in responding."

For Saudi Arabia, a top oil producer, the Red Sea had emerged a critical shipping alternative to the ​war-blockaded Strait of Hormuz.

Skip next section Welcome to our coverage

Welcome to our coverage

After the Strait of Hormuz, the conflict has now embroiled another one of the world's vital energy shipping corridors — the Red Sea.

Earlier this week, Yemen's Iran-backed Houthi rebels announced a blockade of Saudi vessels in the Red Sea, and then claimed strikes on two Saudi oil tankers for violating it.

The Saudi-led coalition in Yemen responded on Friday by attacking the Houthi-held Yemeni port city of Hodeida. The coalition said it had only targeted "military" sites linked to threats against commercial shipping in the Red Sea.

But the Houthis accused the coalition of targeting civilian infrastructure and have now said they would retaliate against Saudi Arabia.

Before we dive in further on the deepening crisis in the Middle East, here is a round-up of developments in the region on Friday:

  • The US launched strikes on Iran for the 13th consecutive night. Iranian state media reported explosions across the country
  • US President Donald Trump said Iran will pay the financial cost of any damage to ships or cargo amid the dispute over the Strait of Hormuz
  • Trump also claimed that Tehran is getting "very serious" in its discussions with the US
  • On the other hand, Iran's Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said Tehran would hold any country assisting the US in an attack on the Islamic republic, accountable
  • The Houthi rebel group in Yemen denied that it was completely closing the Bab al-Mandeb Strait, which links the Red Sea to the Gulf of Aden and the Indian Ocean

Stay tuned as we bring you the latest on the US-Iran war and the Middle East.

entries.title: Trump addresses rescheduled White House Correspondents' Dinner
entries.summary: The event was originally scheduled for April but was disrupted by the alleged attempted assassination of Donald Trump. His hourlong speech combined jokes with attacks on members of the press.
entries.content:
United States of America

Trump speaks at delayed White House Correspondents' Dinner

July 25, 2026

The event was originally scheduled for April but was disrupted by the alleged attempted assassination of Donald Trump. His hourlong speech combined jokes with attacks on members of the press.

US President Donald Trump addressed hundreds of journalists at a scaled-down and rescheduled White House Correspondents' Dinner on Friday night.

The gala was held amid heightened security measures, three months after the original event was cut short by an alleged attempt to assassinate Trump.

Trump delivered the speech at Washington's Waldorf Astoria, a smaller venue that held only about 700 people, instead of its usual venue, the Washington Hilton.

Trump jokes about possible third term

"Just like my presidency, the second time is always better. It's always better," Trump said. "And the third time will be better yet."

"I'm only kidding," he added.

Trump has repeatedly suggested that he would entertain the idea of a third term, despite the 22nd Amendment of the US Constitution barring a president from being elected more than twice.

Trump makes light of shooting incident, praises Secret Service officer

Trump also joked about the incident during April's gala, when a gunman tried to storm a security checkpoint before he was stopped by security personnel before making it into the ballroom where the dinner was being held.

"After hearing the gunshots, many people yelled, 'Get down! Get down!', which caused Nicki Minaj to start twerking. Do you believe it? Get down!" Trump said.

The president also praised Victor Gonzalez, the Secret Service officer who was shot during the April confrontation with the suspect. "What he did was amazing," Trump said. "We salute you and we thank you with all of our hearts."

What else did Trump say during the White House Correspondents' Dinner?

This year's events were the first Trump has attended as president. He did not appear at any correspondents' dinners during his first term.

Trump said he had not attended previous dinners because the press has treated him "unfairly," although he promised to come back next year.

The US president has long had a hostile relationship with many journalists and media outlets .

During his speech, he attacked some journalists, including CNN's Kaitlan Collins — whom Trump repeatedly complained about not smiling enough — and Josh Dawsey of The Wall Street Journal. Both were honored with journalism awards at the gala.

Despite those barbs, Trump ended his speech, which lasted over an hour, by saying that he has "tremendous respect" for the reporters attending the dinner.

"I have tremendous respect for the people in this room. Sometimes I don't feel you treat me fair. Maybe you do. I don't know," Trump said.

Trump vs the media

The Trump administration has filed lawsuits against multiple media outlets, barred the Associated Press from the White House ​press pool and limited journalists' access ‌to the Pentagon, among other measures.

Trump has maintained that the measures aim to improve accountability and address media bias.

Speaking in the Oval Office on Friday, he defended federal subpoenas — which were later withdrawn — issued to New York Times journalists over their reporting on the security of the new Qatari-donated Air Force One.

"We're not after journalists. We're after leakers. We're after people that are cowards, people that are unpatriotic, people that ⁠are treasonous in many cases. And the way ​you find them is through the journalists," Trump said.

Edited by: Karl Sexton

entries.title: Starship completes 1st test flight since SpaceX IPO
entries.summary: Starship splashed down in the Indian Ocean to complete its 13th test flight and its first since Elon Musk's SpaceX went public in June.
entries.content:
July 25, 2026

Starship splashed down in the Indian Ocean to complete its 13th test flight and its first since Elon Musk's SpaceX went public in June.

SpaceX's Starship megarocket completed a test flight on Friday, the first since Elon Musk's company went public on Wall Street in June.

The ship splashed down into the Indian Ocean, which was celebrated by SpaceX employees watching along from the firm's headquarters in Starbase, Texas.

"Starship is intact, floating in the ocean and transmitting telemetry!" Musk said on X.

This was the world's most powerful rocket's 13th flight.

Previous tests had ended with Starship in flames or exploding at splashdown, or breaking up in midair.

What do we know about the latest SpaceX Starship test?

Starship, which is around 122 meters (400 feet) tall, deployed 20 Starlink satellites into suborbital space.

After ​briefly contacting SpaceX's network of around 10,000 orbiting satellites, they reentered Earth's ​atmosphere and burned up as planned.

The hourlong test "will provide critical data as we prepare to expand our Starlink constellation" of the company's satellite internet service, SpaceX said.

By the end of 2026, SpaceX aims to use the Starship rocket to expand its Starlink network with the latest V3 satellites, providing coverage in remote areas where traditional cellular networks are unavailable.

Edited by: Karl Sexton

entries.title: Iran war: Saudi-led coalition attacks Yemen's Hodeida port city
entries.summary: The strikes come after the Iran-backed Houthis attacked several Saudi oil tankers in the Red Sea in recent days. The escalation comes as the US and Iran also vie for control of the vital Strait of Hormuz. DW has more.
entries.content:
Middle East

Iran war: Saudi-led coalition attacks Yemen's Hodeida

Published July 24, 2026last updated July 25, 2026

The strikes come after the Iran-backed Houthis attacked several Saudi oil tankers in the Red Sea in recent days. The escalation comes as the US and Iran also vie for control of the vital Strait of Hormuz. DW has more.

Skip next section What you need to know

What you need to know

This blog has ended. Thank you for joining us.

For the latest on the US-Iran war on Friday, July, head over to our blog.

Below are the main developments on the US war with Iran and news from the Middle East on Friday, July 24:  

  • Saudi-led coalition strikes the Houthi-held Yemeni port city of Hodeida
  • The attacks come after Yemen's Iran-backed Houthi rebels claimed several strikes on Saudi oil tankers as part of itsRed Seablockade
  • The Houthisclaim Bab al-Mandeb Strait is not closed, saying the blockade only targets Saudi ships
  • EU naval mission ASPIDES raises risk level for merchant ships in Red Seadue to Houthi actions
  • This comes as the US and Iranvie for control over theStrait of Hormuz, another key regional passageway for energy exports
  • Israeli prime minister Benjamin Netanyahu vows to 'act with full force' after fatal West Bank clashes
  • USconducts strikes on Iran for 13th consecutive night; Iran says IRGC base in northern Iran was attacked

Tired of missing our real-time updates? Click here to add us as a Preferred Source on Google. Then tap the "Star" or "Preferred" to keep DW News at the top of your feed.

Skip next section We are ending our coverage

We are ending our coverage

Thank you for reading. Join us for more daily coverage of the US-Iran war and developments from the region in our blog on Saturday.

Skip next section US forces 'disable' vessel which attempted to breach blockade of Iranian ports

US forces 'disable' vessel which attempted to breach blockade of Iranian ports

US forces have "disabled" a merchant vessel that attempted to circumvent the US blockade on Iranian ports, military sources told the Associated Press news agency.

US Central Command spokesperson Tim Hawkins told AP that the M/T Lavine was "disabled" in the Gulf of Oman on Friday, after the vessel had reportedly attempted to circumvent the US blockade four times.

Hawkins claimed the ship did not comply with US commands after it was warned. Hawkins said US forces then fired into the ship's engine room.

It's the second commercial vessel attacked by the US since the military reimposed its blockade on Iranian ports on July 14. It follows the collapse of a ceasefire between the US and Iran on July 8. 

US President Donald Trump first imposed a blockade on Iran's ports in April, before it was paused during the ceasefire following the US-Iran Memorandum of Understanding in June.    

Skip next section Bahrain activates alarm sirens amid reports that US naval facility targeted by Iran

Bahrain activates alarm sirens amid reports that US naval facility targeted by Iran

The Bahraini Interior Ministry said sirens were being sounded late Friday night.

"Citizens and residents are urged to remain calm and head to the nearest safe place," the ministry posted on X.

Bahrain is home to a US military base known as Naval Support Activity Bahrain. Bahrain has frequently been targeted in Iranian attacks since the outbreak of the US-Iran war on February 28. 

Reports on X suggested there were explosions near the base, and that it might have been hit by an Iranian missile. The US military has not commented on the incident.

Skip next section Saudi-led coalition confirms attacks on Hodeida, but said it did not hit city's port

Saudi-led coalition confirms attacks on Hodeida, but said it did not hit city's port

The Saudi-led coalition confirmed attacks on Hodeida in comments carried by Saudi broadcaster Al-Arabiya.

The coalition, however, said it did not strike the city's port and had only targeted "military" sites.

"All ports in the governorate remain open to shipping," the statement said. "The coalition adds that the destroyed targets were linked to threats against commercial shipping in the Red Sea."

Skip next section Saudi attacks Houthi-held Hodeida, rebel-aligned media says

Saudi attacks Houthi-held Hodeida, rebel-aligned media says

Saudi Arabia has attacked Hodeida, according to media aligned with the Houthi rebel movement in Yemen.

The Houthis control the port city.

"A Saudi aggression comprising a series of airstrikes hit facilities belonging to the telecommunications authority," the Houthi-aligned Al-Masirah TV channel reported. Al-Masirah operates from southern Beirut.

In addition, the Saudis reportedly struck Kamaran Island in the Red Sea, which the Houthis also control.

The attacks come after the Houthis claimed responsibility for strikes on several Saudi oil tankers in the Red Sea in recent days. The Houthis say they are blockading Saudi vessels in the Red Sea.

Saudi's official SPA news agency reported that a Saudi vessel was again targeted on Friday, and there is "minor damage to the vessel's hull" as a result.

Skip next section Trump claims that Iranians are getting 'very serious' in discussions with US

Trump claims that Iranians are getting 'very serious' in discussions with US

Taking questions from journalists in the Oval Office, US President Donald Trump claimed that Iran is getting "very serious" in its discussions with the US.

Trump was asked about reports that the US could soon launch a large-scale attack on Iran, the biggest of the war so far. 

"No, I haven't," Trump replied when asked by journalists if he had decided to launch the operation.

"Look, we're talking to them right now. I think they're getting more and more serious as the days go by," Trump said.

Iranian officials have not commented on whether talks are underway with the US. A ceasefire deal between the US and Iran fell apart on July 8.  

Trump has repeatedly claimed Iran has been close to agreeing terms with the US since the start of the war in late February.  

Skip next section WATCH — US strikes Iran for 13th straight night

WATCH — US strikes Iran for 13th straight night

US Central Command has said the attacks targeted military capabilities threatening commercial shipping, while Iran has claimed Washington has deployed advanced weapons against the country.

The UN warned the conflict could spiral out of control, as both sides adopt increasingly confrontational rhetoric and the risk of wider regional escalation grows.

Skip next section Trump says China, Russia not selling weapons to Iran

Trump says China, Russia not selling weapons to Iran

In a post on Truth Social, US President Donald Trump claimed the leaders of China and Russia told him their countries are not selling weapons to Iran and that he believes them.

"President Xi, at our recent meeting in Beijing, China, told me that he would not, under any circumstances, give or sell Weapons to the Islamic Republic of Iran — And that statement included Chinese Companies," Trump said. "I take him at his word, and, besides, I am doing him very big favors, also.

"Likewise, President Putin, despite the the horrible war going on in Ukraine (The relationship remains, as it does with President Zelenskyy), told me he would not sell Weapons to Iran," Trump said.

Trump said China and Russia are not participating in the Iran war, and "if they did, it would be very bad for them — Certainly not in their best interests."

Reuters news agency reported this week that US intelligence officials are probing whether Russia is helping Iran target CIA facilities in the Middle East.

CNN reported in April that US intelligence indicated that China is preparing weapons shipments to Iran amid a ceasefire. China has denied shipping weapons to Iran amid the war. 

Skip next section Houthis on Saudi maritime blockade: 'There is no closure of Bab al-Mandeb'

Houthis on Saudi maritime blockade: 'There is no closure of Bab al-Mandeb'

Yemen's Houthi rebel group has denied that it is completely closing the Bab al-Mandeb Strait. 

"There is no closure of Bab al-Mandeb as some are suggesting," Houthi spokesperson Mohammed Abdusalam posted on X. He said the group is just engaged in a "naval blockade targeting only the Saudi side."

The Houthis have alleged that Saudi Arabia is sieging Yemeni areas that the group controls, and in turn have begun their "naval blockade" of Saudi vessels.  

The Houthis are an Iran-backed group and designated as a terrorist organization by the US, Canada and several other countries. They control large swathes of western and northern Yemen, including the capital Sanaa and the coastline along the Red Sea.   

The Bab al-Mandeb Strait links the Red Sea to the Gulf of Aden and the Indian Ocean. It is a particularly important passageway for Saudi Arabia to export its crude oil.

Insecurity in the Strait of Hormuz has caused Saudi Arabia to shift its oil exports to the western port city of Yanbu, where the crude is then shipped via the Bab al-Mandeb Strait.    

Crude prices in recent days have temporarily spiked above $100 (almost €88) for the first time since May due to the crises both in the Strait of Hormuz and Bab al-Mandeb.

The Houthis have claimed attacks on Saudi oil tankers in the Red Sea in recent days.

The EU naval operation ASPIDES has raised its threat level in the Bab al-Mandeb Strait for merchant ships, and said the risk of escalation remains high.

Skip next section UN urges repatriation of 6,000 sailors stranded in Strait of Hormuz

UN urges repatriation of 6,000 sailors stranded in Strait of Hormuz

The United Nations has called on countries involved in the Middle East war to help repatriate around 6,000 sailors who remain stranded on ships in the Strait of Hormuz.

UN rights chief Volker Türk called on states to urgently provide consular assistance to stranded seafarers, deliver essential supplies, and "facilitate safe passage for stranded seafarers to safely evacuate and disembark."

"Attacks against civilian vessels are unacceptable and must stop. They are protected under international humanitarian law," Türk's spokesperson told reporters. "Seafarers remain exposed to hostilities as deadly attacks in the strait continue — facing imminent risks of death or harm."

The UN rights office said 17 ship crew members had been reported killed since the conflict erupted in late February.

It said at least 93 other sailors, across nine ships, had been abandoned at sea by their ship owners.

"Thee seafarers have been left on their ships to fend for themselves without food, water, fuel, medical care, electricity or means to communicate with their families," Türk's spokesperson said.

Skip next section Netanyahu vows to 'act with full force' after fatal West Bank clashes

Netanyahu vows to 'act with full force' after fatal West Bank clashes

The Israeli military killed four Palestinians near an Israeli settlement in the occupied West Bank on Friday, while two Israelis were also killed in the clashes.

Israeli media reports and local Palestinian officials suggested that a group of Israeli settlers, some of whom were armed, entered the Palestinian village of Tell, southwest of Nablus, on Friday morning. The settlers were met by residents of the Palestinian village who were fearful of an attack.

Footage of the incident that was confirmed by the Israeli military and shared online by the military correspondent for Israel's Army Radio showed two armed men in civilian clothing, as well as at least one Israeli soldier, pointing their weapons at a group of Palestinians who had gathered in a field.

"Villagers came out to defend their homes and property. Clashes and physical altercations broke out between the residents and the settlers," the head of the village council in Tell, Walid Zidan, told the AFP news agency.

"Israeli soldiers were present and together with the settlers began opening fire ... it was the settlers who stormed the village, with the intention of killing, vandalizing and setting property on fire."

The Israeli military said it has received reports that Israeli civilians were hiking in the area and had been attacked by Palestinians.

In response to the incident, Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu vowed to "act with full force against the terrorists and those who orchestrate and sponsor them."

The Israeli military subsequently set up roadblocks near Tell and Nablus and announced a widespread operation in the occupied West Bank.

"Following the terror attack earlier today in the area of Tell, IDF soldiers are preparing for extensive counterterrorism operational activity in the sector," the military said.

Skip next section Blasts heard near Irbil airport in Iraqi Kurdistan

Blasts heard near Irbil airport in Iraqi Kurdistan

Blasts were heard near Irbil's airport in Iraqi Kurdistan on Friday, news agencies reported citing their journalists on the ground.

The Associated Press said its journalist heard at least seven blasts around 9:30 a.m. (0630 GMT) and observed at least four plumes of black smoke from areas near or inside a military base at the city's airport. The base hosts US forces in northern Iraq.

An AFP journalist observed drones hovering over the city, with air defenses activated.

According to the Reuters news agency, a drone crashed near Irbil International Airport, prompting a temporary flight suspension.

Irbil is the capital of Iraq's semi-autonomous Kurdish region.

Skip next section US attacked IRGC base in north: state media

US attacked IRGC base in north: state media

Iran said that the US military hit a Revolutionary Guards' (IRGC) base in the northern province of Gilan, according to the state media.

"This morning, an IRGC naval forces headquarters in Zibakenar was targeted by American enemy projectiles, which damaged some of the equipment in the complex," said Ali Bagheri, deputy governor for the province, quoted by the official IRNA news agency.

He added, "Based on initial investigations, no reports of human casualties have been received so far, and the various aspects of this incident are being investigated by the relevant authorities."

Skip next section Iran's FM Abbas Araghchi warns countries assisting US attacks

Iran's FM Abbas Araghchi warns countries assisting US attacks

Speaking at the Shanghai Cooperation Organization summit in Kyrgyzstan, Iran's Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said Tehran would hold accountable any country assisting the US in an attack on the Islamic republic.

"Any participation, cooperation or assistance in committing aggression against Iran will create international responsibility for the relevant parties," Araghchi said, adding that Iran "reserves its right to take all necessary measures within the framework of self-defense."

He said the source of any aggression against Iran would be considered as a legitimate target of Iran's defense forces.

Skip next section US strikes on southwest kill at least four people, says Iran

US strikes on southwest kill at least four people, says Iran

The overnight US attack on the province of Khuzestan in southwestern Iran killed at least four people and injured several others, Iran's official IRNA news agency reported.

Khuzestan deputy Governor Valiollah Hayati said that the US missile attack hit areas around provincial capital Ahvaz.

"Four of our compatriots were martyred and five others were injured," IRNA cited Hayati as saying.

entries.title: Paramount agrees to delay Warner Bros. merger amid lawsuit
entries.summary: Paramount has agreed to freeze its merger with Warner Bros. Discovery until as late as June 2027. Twelve states have argued that the deal would create a "media behemoth" that would harm the US entertainment industry.
entries.content:
July 25, 2026

Paramount has agreed to freeze its merger with Warner Bros. Discovery until as late as June 2027. Twelve states have argued that the deal would create a "media behemoth" that would harm the US entertainment industry.

Paramount on Friday agreed to delay its merger with Warner Bros. Discovery as a lawsuit from a dozen US states seeking to block the deal altogether moves forward.

In a court filing, Paramount said it would pause the $110 billion (€96.69 billion) deal until June 2027.

Friday's agreement is a "significant win because the result is exactly what we have sought from the outset: a direct path to a trial based on the evidence," according to Paramount, which was bought by Skydance last year.

"This is the fastest and clearest way to prove that this transaction is good for competition, good for consumers and good for creators," the company added.

Judge pauses Paramount and Warner Bros megamerger

The move comes just days after a US federal judge temporarily blocked the proposed merger following a lawsuit brought by 12 states.

The states raised "serious questions" about the deal's potential to "substantially lessen competition," the judge said in her ruling, adding that "the balance of equities and public interest tip sharply in favor of the Plaintiff States."

The Trump administration approved the merger of Paramount Skydance, controlled by the Ellison family who are close allies of US President Donald Trump, and Warner Bros. Discovery, the parent company of CNN and HBO, on June 12 without demanding any changes.

States suing to block merger welcome decision

Twelve states led by California filed a lawsuit on July 13, arguing that the deal would create a "media behemoth" that would damage the US entertainment and media industry.

"We are eager to continue to make our case in court and celebrate another tremendous win in our effort to ensure this unlawful merger never sees the light of day," California Attorney General Rob Bonta said in a statement on Friday.

The other 11 states joining the lawsuit — all of them Democratic-led — are Arizona, Colorado, Connecticut, Massachusetts, Minnesota, Nevada, New Jersey, New Mexico, New York, Oregon and Washington.

"From the workers and artists who bring stories to life to the families who buy tickets at the box office, Paramount's illegal takeover of Warner Bros. is a bad deal for all those who count on a competitive entertainment industry," said New York Attorney General Letitia James on Friday.

Edited by: Karl Sexton

entries.title: ICC votes to dismiss Chief Prosecutor Karim Khan
entries.summary: Members of the International Criminal Court have voted to remove Chief Prosecutor Karim Khan amid allegations of sexual misconduct. Khan has denied the accusations.
entries.content:
Law and JusticeGlobal issues

ICC votes to dismiss Chief Prosecutor Karim Khan

July 24, 2026

Members of the International Criminal Court have voted to remove Chief Prosecutor Karim Khan amid allegations of sexual misconduct. Khan has denied the accusations.

International Criminal Court members voted on Friday to dismiss Karim Khan as prosecutor ​following allegations ​of sexual misconduct. 

The ICC's oversight body, the Assembly of States Parties (ASP), found that Khan had committed "serious misconduct and serious breach of duty," ASP President Paivi Kaukoranta said.

What do we know about the Khan allegations?

A British barrister, Khan was accused of sexual misconduct by a female aide, allegations which he has repeatedly denied.

He had been temporarily removed from his duties at the ICC in June, following a report by the executive committee of the court's oversight body that found he had committed "serious misconduct."

In all, 82 of the court's ​125 member states voted in favor of Khan's removal, while 13 voted against and 15 countries abstained.

Khan, 56, made headlines in 2024 when he successfully applied for arrest warrants against Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and former Defense Minister Yoav Gallant over the Gaza war, as well as leading members of the Hamas militant group who have since been killed. Hamas carried out the October 7, 2023 terror attacks on Israel. 

All active ICC warrants will remain in place despite Khan's dismissal, because only ICC judges have the authority to withdraw warrants.

What were the reactions to Khan's dismissal?

Khan's lawyer, Tayab Ali, said Khan would challenge his dismissal.

"Mr. Khan will challenge the lawfulness and fairness of the decision, though all available legal mechanisms," Ali wrote in a post on X.

Kenneth Roth, the former executive director of Human Rights Watch and now a visiting professor at Princeton University, wrote on X that the ICC states did "the right thing" by removing Khan.

Israel's Ambassador to the UN, Danny Danon, criticized Khan, suggesting the barrister had thought that the arrest warrants against Israeli officials, which Danon called a "political witch hunt," would "distract from serious sexual misconduct allegations."

"He was wrong," Danon said.

Khan suspension comes as Trump administration wants to 'dismantle' ICC

The move to dismiss Khan also comes at a time when the US President Donald Trump's administration is seeking to weaken and undermine the ICC. The court, based in the Dutch city of The Hague, investigates and prosecutes individuals for genocide and other crimes against humanity. 

US Secretary of State Marco Rubio recently said that the US had begun a "sweeping campaign to dismantle the threat posed by the International Criminal Court to US sovereignty."

The State Department said countries that enjoy the benefits of the US security umbrella are "called upon to reject the ICC's purported authority to prosecute American officials and servicemen." The State Department is also mulling "visa revocations and travel bans for ICC personnel" along with "increased sanctions against the ICC and affiliated organizations."   

Neither the United States nor Israel is a member of the ICC.

Venezuela announces it will withdraw from ICC

Meanwhile, Venezuela said it would withdraw from the ICC on Friday. The move comes after Venezuelan leader Nicolas Maduro was abducted and overthrown by the US earlier this year and replaced by interim leader Delcy Rodriguez, who has been willing to comply with the Trump administration's demands.

Venezuelan Foreign Minister Felix Plasencia said the "court's actions reflect a demonstrated geographical bias, which disproportionately concentrated its work on African and Latin American countries, to the detriment of the Global South."

Plasencia said the withdrawal was at the instruction of Delcy Rodriguez.

Edited by: Wesley Dockery and Karl Sexton

entries.title: Poland's main opposition collapses over far-right slide
entries.summary: A power struggle within Poland's main opposition force has come to a head. But a move to expel former Prime Minister Mateusz Morawiecki may greatly weaken the right-wing party's popularity.
entries.content:
Poland

Poland's main opposition collapses over far-right slide

July 24, 2026

A power struggle within Poland's main opposition force has come to a head. But a move to expel former Prime Minister Mateusz Morawiecki may greatly weaken the right-wing party's popularity.

"Over 30 delegates of our group have effectively forfeited their membership," Jaroslaw Kaczynski, the head of the Law and Justice (PiS) party, said on Friday. He's accusing Poland's former Prime Minister Mateusz Morawiecki, as well as dozens of his followers, of attempting to split the party.

"We couldn't accept that," Kaczynski continued. "It's all done." For their part, the rebels alleged they have not resigned but been "expelled."

A three-hour "last chance" talk between Kaczynski and Morawiecki ended on Thursday without results. "We were looking for understanding, but couldn't accept subjugation," Piotr Mueller, an EU delegate close to Morawiecki, later said about the talks on X.

The ultimatum that Kacynski had placed on rebel party members ended at midnight. By then, they were expected to deliver a written declaration that they would refrain from activities in the Rozwoj Plus (Development Plus) association led by Morawiecki. In Kaczynski's view, the breakaway association has undermined his party's primacy.

"I'm not signing any loyalty pledge," Morawiecki told the Polish television station TVN. "That's something one might have required of me in the 1980s," he added, alluding to his persecution for his father's prominent opposition to the regime at the time.

For a quarter of a century, Kaczynski and his PiS party have dominated the right wing of Poland's party landscape. Any attempt to establish a new, more radical right was successfully quashed. Since 2001, PiS has been in power twice, from 2005-2007 and again from 2015-2023, and has occupied the office of state president with Kaczynski's twin brother, Lech, then Andrzej Duda and — since mid-2025 — Karol Nawrocki. 

Greatest crisis since party's founding

Just over a year before the next parliamentary election, the party is facing its greatest crisis since it got its start in 2001.

By now, two parties have established themselves to the right of PiS: the far-right nationalist and libertarian alliance Confederation Liberty and Independence (KWIN), and the extreme right-wing, ultranationalist, traditionalist Confederation of the Polish Crown (KKP). Taken together, they enjoy more support in the polls than the PiS party alone. Kaczynski's party has lost many voters to these two radical groups.

To win them back, Kaczynski has pushed his party ever further to the right. In March, he nominated Przemyslaw Czarnek, the ultraconservative, ultra-Catholic former minister of education and science, as the party's lead candidate for the 2027 parliamentary election. Morawiecki and his followers have called the move a fundamental mistake.

Two lungs or one fist?

Czarnek is trying to outflank the two confederation parties from the right with verbal attacks against the EU and Ukraine. In the recent Polish-Ukrainian dispute over unresolved historical issues, Czarnek called for all military aid to Ukraine to be halted until Kyiv changed its position. Supporters of this hard line have said the party should act "like a fist."

Morawiecki responded to his party's shift to the right by launching the political association Development Plus. He's invited 1,000 guests from various political backgrounds to a policy event in late July, where they can discuss the country's future over a barbecue.

The former prime minister has been traveling up and down the country to speak with local politicians and businesses. As early as April, he clashed with Kaczynski, who accused him of threatening the party's unity. At the time, however, the party head gone along with Morawiecki's efforts and spoke of "two lungs" within the PiS party. That compromise did not hold long.

Reaching out to new voters

At public appearances, Morawiecki has repeatedly emphasized that he intends to remain within the PiS party. His goal, he said, was to open the party to new voters, to ensure that right-wing conservatives returned to power in 2027.

Just a few days ago, Morawiecki could count on the support of 40 members of Poland's lower house of parliament, the Sejm, and several EU delegates. But it's currently unclear whether all will be able to withstand Kaczynski's pressure.

Opinion polls conducted by Opinia24 for the Polish channels TVN and TVN24 on July 22 gave Morawiecki 6.2% of the vote, while support for PiS dropped to 17.7%. In the 2023 parliamentary election, the PiS party under Kaczynski won 35% of the vote.

Out of all of Kaczynski's longtime associates who have worked with him since the 1990s, Morawiecki is still considered an outsider. Following Poland's democratic transition, the trained historian held leading positions in several banks before joining the PiS party in 2016.

Under PiS party rule he served as development minister and finance minister, and finally prime minister. Morawiecki and his associates have accused their opponents of orchestrating a plot against them. 

Gloating among the governing coalition

The center-right governing coalition under current Prime Minister Donald Tusk has made no secret of its amusement with the PiS party's current predicament. "I love PiS so much, I'd love to have two of them," Foreign Minister Radoslaw Sikorski joked when he heard the news..

Political scientist Danuta Plecka said Friday that the situation was like "a gift" to the ruling government. "All the scandals of recent months are now fading into the background," she explained. "Tusk doesn't have to do anything, he can just sit by the riverbank and wait for the bodies to float by."

However, University of Gdansk researcher believes the conflict between Kaczynski and Morawiecki may be a staged performance. "There are hardly and programmatic differences between the two," she told TVN. "The main difference between them is in the language and political tactics."

She believes Morawiecki is meant to win over voters who lean more toward the political center. Then, after the election, both groups could work together, Plecka predicted.

This article was originally written in German.

entries.title: Trump threatens EU with tariff probe over Google, tech fines
entries.summary: US President Donald Trump has said he will initiate a tariff investigation against the EU in response to fines against US tech companies. He cited the latest case that Google lost on Thursday, as well as others.
entries.content:
Europe

Trump threatens EU with tariff probe over Google, tech fines

July 24, 2026

US President Donald Trump has said he will initiate a tariff investigation against the EU in response to fines against US tech companies. He cited the latest case that Google lost on Thursday, as well as others.

US President Donald Trump on Friday threatened to launch a tariff investigation against the EU in response to the bloc's anti-competition fines and other penalties levied against US tech giants like Google, Apple, Amazon and Meta. 

In particular, he cited Thursday's latest fine of €890 million (roughly $1 billion) issued against Google for allegedly giving unfair preference to its own search engine and its Play app. 

Trump's threats come just a few hours after his administration imposed its latest tariffs on the EU, and many other countries, for supposedly not doing enough to prevent imports made using forced labor from their supply chains.

US trading partners and allies like the EU, Japan and Australia have responded to these with a mixture of outrage and bafflement at the new tariffs.

What did Trump say online?

Trump issued the warning in a lengthy post on his Truth Social online platform.

"The European Union is at it again and, as usual, taking direct aim at GREAT American Companies!," he wrote. 

He then listed a series of fines — or cumulative totals of supposed fines — against various tech companies, which he falsely alleged were issued "for no reason at all" and "without explanation."

He mentioned the latest penalty to hit Google, and claimed this took the total of their fines to "over 18 Billion Dollars!" without specifying a timeframe or evidence of any sort.

EU courts did recently uphold a record fine of over $4 billion for Google — in a process that had been under review for almost eight years — in one case among several in recent years.

"The United States of America is not a 'PIGGYBANK' for Europe, nor will we allow it to be! Please let this TRUTH serve to represent that we will immediately initiate a 301 Investigation in the practice of 'ROBBING' American Companies and, in turn, the American Taxpayer," Trump wrote.

What is a 301 Investigation?

The 301 Investigations are the new means Trump relies on to impose tariffs, after the Supreme Court declared he had overstepped his authority with the near-global levies he imposed on what he called "Liberation Day" in 2025.

The so-called investigation relies on the US internally demonstrating what it deems to be unfair trade practices against it in order to issue retaliatory sanctions and refers to Section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974. Dozens of such investigations are in the pipeline.

"The European Union will pay a very big price for this illegal and highly unethical conduct, which I have consistently warned them about," Trump wrote. "The penalties will be entirely reveresed and, we anticipate, a substantial TARIFF to be placed on them at the earlier moment. Stay tuned!"

US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer had already criticized the decision on Thursday, saying the EU's enforcement action undermined "constructive dialogue" and posed a "real risk" to transatlantic trade stability.

The EU and US have been bickering over the terms of their fragile trade agreement reached last year amid Trump's Liberation Day tariff frenzy. The slow ratification process across the EU's 27-plus member states and the institutions in Brussels has frustrated the Trump White House.

Edited by: Sean Sinico
